name: Ivan Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me, Ivan. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. What you say is confidential. Could you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for Kessler and Sons, a family firm, three vans, been going since the seventies. We do farms, old farmhouses, the village hall, the church when the heating trips. Old Mr Kessler still writes the jobs in a big diary on the office desk, and I like it that way.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like old houses, you open a wall and find cloth-covered wiring from before my grandfather was born, and you put it right. What wears me out is customers who've watched a video and think they know better. Pay's good, I've got well over a year saved, and my grandmother left me her cottage on Mill Lane, so Greta and I will live there when we're married next summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. That's what I've been saying all along.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was a lot of noise from people who sit at computers. At the pub I'd say I never touched the thing and I didn't miss out on anything. I don't go online much, so that's where I'd say it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means the world stays the way I like it. Mr Kessler keeps his diary, farmers keep calling when the milking parlour trips, and I keep my job. Greta's bank might use it for some forms, but nothing that costs her the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as now. I'd keep putting money aside every month and do up the cottage, new consumer unit, rewire upstairs, before the wedding. I wouldn't change a thing about how I work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Content. Relieved, maybe, but mostly content.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you never touched AI. Has anyone pushed you to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Young Tom Kessler (the boss's grandson) wanted to put the bookings on a tablet with some AI thing. His grandfather said no, and I backed the old man up. A diary doesn't run out of battery in a cowshed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the biggest worry in your life right now, AI aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the wedding costs and getting the cottage done in time. And Mr Kessler is seventy-four, so one day the firm changes hands. But in this picture that's just ordinary life.

say: I'd say at the pub it was **noise** from people at computers.
I'd say he **never touched** AI and missed nothing.
think: Privately, the world stays **as he likes** it, with diaries and farm callouts.
Greta's **bank job** might change a little but stays safe.
do: Carry on working **exactly as now** for Kessler and Sons.
Rewire and fit a **new consumer unit** in the cottage before the wedding.
S0.quote: A diary doesn't run out of battery in a cowshed.
fieldNote: He is **proud** of not using AI and sides with the old boss against it.
His real worries are ordinary: **wedding costs** and the boss's age.
An inherited cottage gives him **unusual security** for his age.

steps.text: Rewire the upstairs of the Mill Lane cottage before the wedding
Keep putting money aside every month for the wedding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hm. That sounds like the office lot getting their comeuppance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the people at desks who need to worry, not tradesmen. I'd say it at the pub and at church, and I'd tell the young lads to get an apprenticeship instead of going to university. That's what my father told me, and he was right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it worries me for Greta more than me. My fiancée Greta processes mortgage paperwork at the bank in town, and checking and writing forms is exactly what that card says goes first. My job's safe enough, but I'd want her job to be safe too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working as I do, no tablets, no apps. I'd save harder, maybe double what I put away, so if Greta's hours get cut we can still do the wedding properly. And I'd tell her to ask her manager straight out where her job is going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I suppose. Not for me, but for her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Mr Kessler's grandson brings in the AI booking system after all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd use what I have to, and not more. I'm not saying I'd quit over it. But I'd still keep my own notebook in the van, because I trust that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if Greta's job went?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The banks, for chasing profit over people who've worked for them ten years. And the government, for letting it happen without asking anyone. I'm for business, but a business should look after its own.

say: I'd say people at **desks** need to worry, not tradesmen.
I'd tell young lads to get an **apprenticeship**, not a degree.
think: Greta's **mortgage paperwork** job is exactly what the card says goes first.
His own job feels **safe enough**, but the household's doesn't fully.
do: **Double** the monthly savings to protect the wedding.
Get Greta to ask her **manager** where her job is going.
feel: **Uneasy** for Greta rather than for himself.
S1.quote: My fiancée Greta processes mortgage paperwork at the bank in town, and checking and writing forms is exactly what that card says goes first.
fieldNote: His public line blames **office workers**; privately he worries about **Greta**.
He'd accept new tools only **grudgingly**, keeping his own notebook.
He blames **banks and government**, but stays pro-business.

steps.text: Keep working from a paper notebook, without any AI apps
Double the amount saved each month for the wedding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I don't believe that. But go on, I'll play along.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's rubbish, and that people still want a man they can trust in their house. I'd say it at church, at the pub, and to Mr Kessler. I wouldn't say it online, I'm not online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, if it really happened, Greta's job is gone in 2028, no question. Then by 2031, if a robot can rewire a farmhouse, I'm finished too, and I'd be thirty-two with no other trade. I don't know what I'd do, honestly. I've never wanted to do anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save everything I could and stop spending on the cottage beyond what's needed. We'd keep the wedding small, in the village, no big hall. And I'd lean on family, my dad's got the smallholding, so there's always food and work of a sort there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, if I'm honest. I'd lie awake over it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try to learn anything new, with three years before the robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have to think hard about it. Learning computers isn't me. Maybe I'd go for something like inspection, where someone signs a paper, but I'm not sure that's safe either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you want the government to step in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not with handouts, no. But I'd vote for whoever puts the brakes on it and makes companies keep people on. And I'd want proper apprenticeships for something, anything, that still needs a person.

say: I'd say it's **rubbish** and people still want a man they **trust**.
I'd say it at **church and the pub**, never online.
think: Greta's job goes in **2028**, and his own by **2031**.
At thirty-two he'd have **no other trade** and no idea what to do.
do: Save **everything possible** and stop cottage spending beyond essentials.
Keep the wedding **small**, in the village.
Lean on his father's **smallholding** for food and work.
feel: **Frightened**, and he'd lie awake over it.
S2.quote: If a robot can rewire a farmhouse, I'm finished too, and I'd be thirty-two with no other trade.
fieldNote: He opens with **disbelief** but privately expects both incomes gone.
He has **no plan B** and resists learning computers.
He wants **brakes on companies**, not handouts.

steps.text: Put every spare pay packet into savings
Hold a small village wedding instead of a hired hall
Fall back on his father's smallholding for food and work
Vote for whoever makes companies keep people on

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Still too fast for my liking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I'd always say, that people want people in their homes and the old ways last. I'd tell the lads at Kessler not to panic. Maybe I'd say a bit louder that the government should protect apprenticeships.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, five years gives Greta time, she's quick and she could find something else by 2031. For me it's 2034, I'd be thirty-five. That's long enough to save a lot, but I still don't know what a man like me does after that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and save hard, maybe forty per cent of my pay. We'd still marry next summer, but we'd wait on children until we see how it goes. I'd talk to Mr Kessler about whether the firm could do the inspection and certificate side, if that stays human.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but not as bad as the fast one. There's time to get the house in order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait on children. How would Greta take that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd hate it. Greta (my fiancée) wants three, and so do I. But I'm not having children I can't feed, my father never did that and neither will I.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try any AI tools in the meantime?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I'd be watching them, mind. If I saw them in other firms working well, maybe. But not before I have to.

say: I'd say people want **people in their homes**, and the old ways last.
I'd push for the government to **protect apprenticeships**.
think: Greta has time to find **other work** by 2031.
His own trade lasts to about **2034**, and he has no idea what comes after.
do: Save about **forty per cent** of his pay.
Marry next summer but **delay children** until the picture is clear.
Ask Mr Kessler about **inspection and certificate** work.
feel: **Worried**, but less than in the fast picture.
S3.quote: I'm not having children I can't feed, my father never did that and neither will I.
fieldNote: Delaying children is a **painful choice** for a man who wants three.
He still **won't try AI**, only watch others.
He sees the **certificate side** as possibly human, but isn't sure.

steps.text: Save about forty per cent of each month's pay
Put off having children until robots' impact is clearer
Ask Mr Kessler about taking on inspection and certificate work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Well. A lot can happen in ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and half of these predictions never come true. I'd tell people at church to get on with their lives. I'd vote for people who care about trades and families, same as always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be forty in 2039, with children by then, so it still hits me in the middle of everything. But I'd have the cottage paid off, years of savings, and maybe the firm, if Mr Kessler's family sells it to me. That's something to stand on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, marry, have children as we planned. I'd ask Mr Kessler about buying into the firm, slowly. And I'd keep saving, a good chunk every month, because the robots will come eventually even if I don't want them to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at the back of my mind. But I'd sleep fine most nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why buy into the firm if robots are coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a firm has customers who trust it, and trust takes fifty years to build. Maybe the robots work for the firm one day, I don't know. But I'd rather own something than be owned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you lean on, if it came to the worst?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Family first, my dad and my brother. Then the church, they've always helped people round here. Not the government, not if I can help it.

say: I'd say **ten years** is long and most predictions fail.
I'd tell people at church to **get on** with their lives.
think: In 2039 he'd be **forty** with children, so it still hits mid-life.
A paid-off cottage, **savings** and maybe the firm give him footing.
do: Ask Mr Kessler about **buying into** the firm slowly.
Keep saving **a good chunk** every month.
feel: **Uneasy** at the back of his mind, but sleeping fine.
S4.quote: A firm has customers who trust it, and trust takes fifty years to build.
fieldNote: Ten years lets him keep **family plans** intact.
He'd rather **own** a firm than depend on government help.
He leans on **family and church** before the state.

steps.text: Marry next summer and start a family as planned
Ask Mr Kessler about buying into the firm over time
Keep saving a fixed sum every month

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Greta out of work and me three years behind her, with no other trade. What would help is apprenticeships that still lead somewhere, and laws that make firms keep people on for a while instead of throwing them out overnight.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what young tradesmen are told. Everyone said a trade was the safe bet, and I believed them. I still do, mostly. People still want a man they can trust in their house.

headlineQuote: Everyone said a trade was the safe bet, and I believed them.
portrait: Ivan is a **27-year-old electrician** at a family firm doing farms and old houses, marrying Greta next summer.
He **never uses AI**, sides with his old boss's paper diary, and trusts family and church.
An **inherited cottage** and a year's savings make him secure in the calm pictures.
His main worry is **Greta's bank job**, which goes first in the faster pictures.
In **AGI by 2028** he is frightened and has no plan B, only savings and family.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with Greta's job gone first and his own three years later.
whatWouldHelp: Laws making firms **keep people on** rather than lay them off overnight.
